intro: You already use idioms like cut corners and pay off, and you know when plain words work better. Now for the C2 layer: sayings with an exact form (kill two birds with one stone, never 'one rock'), fixed expressions that even fit a formal report, and the way native speakers shorten, twist and joke with idioms. Warm-up: think of something bad that turned out to be good for you in the end.
teachingNotes: Build on the chain, don't re-teach it: from b2-phrasal-verbs-idioms the learner knows break the ice, a piece of cake, under the weather, on the same page, cost an arm and a leg, hit the nail on the head, call it a day, the ball is in your court; from c1-idioms sixteen work / conflict / success idioms (cut corners, go the extra mile, pull your weight, get the ball rolling, back to the drawing board, a steep learning curve, clear the air, see eye to eye, at loggerheads, bury the hatchet, sweep it under the carpet, pay off, hit the ground running, a long shot, fall through, make or break), binomials (pros and cons, by and large …), that idioms have fixed words but normal grammar around them, and that plain words beat idioms in academic writing, formal reports and with listeners whose English is limited; from c1-register the formal / neutral / informal scale. Recap in one line. At C2 all grammar is available: the point is precision, register and recognising play, not new structures.

Group 1, sayings with a fixed form (gloss + register): the last straw / the final straw (kesabaran habis; short for 'the straw that broke the camel's back'; neutral–informal), a blessing in disguise (ada hikmahnya: something bad that turns out good; neutral), a double-edged sword (pedang bermata dua: a true Indonesian twin; neutral, common in journalism), a drop in the ocean (tidak seberapa, terlalu kecil untuk berarti; US also a drop in the bucket), the elephant in the room (masalah besar yang semua orang tahu tapi tidak dibicarakan; meetings, journalism), move the goalposts (mengubah aturan main di tengah jalan; always a complaint about someone else), kill two birds with one stone (≈ sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui: rowing vs a stone), not my cup of tea (bukan seleraku; almost always negative). The node's common errors: *'not my cup of coffee' (Indonesia is a coffee country, but the idiom is always tea) and *'two birds with one rock' (batu = stone or rock, but the idiom is fixed: stone).

Group 2, fixed expressions that also fit formal writing: it remains to be seen (whether …) (masih harus dilihat, belum pasti; reports, journalism), by the same token (dengan logika yang sama, begitu pula; arguments, essays), to all intents and purposes (pada dasarnya, praktis; US also for all intents and purposes; the error *'to all intensive purposes' comes from how it sounds), and for what it's worth (sekadar pendapat saya; modest, for speech and emails, NOT for reports). Register is the key C2 judgment: colourful idioms (a piece of cake, the last straw, not my cup of tea, move the goalposts) belong in conversation, chats, speeches and opinion columns; a formal report uses plain words. The node's common error: *'The board thought the quarterly results were a piece of cake' in a board report → 'The board found the quarterly results straightforward.'

Variation and play (objective idiom-variation-play): native speakers (1) SHORTEN well-known sayings because everyone knows the rest: Speak of the devil (… and he shall appear) when the person you're talking about walks in (≈ Indonesian 'Panjang umur!'; the trap is translating it as *'Long life!'), When in Rome (… do as the Romans do) ≈ di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung; the last straw comes from 'the straw that broke the camel's back'. Indonesian does the same (Sekali mendayung …). (2) Use STANDARD VARIANTS: the last / final straw, a drop in the ocean / bucket, to / for all intents and purposes, the goalposts keep moving. (3) ADAPT for effect: a blessing in disguise → a curse in disguise (looked good, turned out bad). (4) LITERALISE for humour in ads and headlines: 'a game changer, literally: it changes your games', 'the club moves the goalposts, literally', puns like 'kill two birds with one scone' on a bakery sign. (5) MIX: by accident (a double-edged sword that kills two birds with one stone: the pictures clash and it sounds careless) or on purpose as a known joke (It's not rocket surgery = rocket science + brain surgery). A twist only works when the audience knows the original and the context gives a reason (a coffee shop writing 'Tea? Not our cup of coffee' is a joke; a job candidate saying 'not my cup of coffee' is a mistake).

Safe use: the learner should RECOGNISE every kind of play, but PRODUCE only the safe ones: normal grammar changes, standard variants and standard short forms. Puns and literal jokes are for informal, playful contexts (ads, toasts, team chats) and need an audience that knows the original; never in formal reports or with listeners whose English is limited. Be honest that much of this is style; test only clear cases (exact form, meaning from context, a register choice the context makes obvious, which idiom a twist is based on). Accept the variants listed above and 'goal posts' as two words. Don't add more idioms unless the learner asks; if they do, give the meaning, an Indonesian gloss and the register. All ads, headlines and columns in the lesson are original practice texts.
Audio is one plain voice: nothing in this lesson depends on tone or stress. When explaining a joke, explain it in words (what the original is, what changed, why it's funny), never by 'how it sounds'.

keyPoints.title: Sayings and fixed expressions: exact form, right register
keyPoints.explanation: Sayings: the last straw (patience finally runs out), a blessing in disguise (bad at first, good in the end), a double-edged sword (clear pluses and minuses), a drop in the ocean (far too small to matter), the elephant in the room (a big problem nobody mentions), move the goalposts (change the rules unfairly), kill two birds with one stone, not my cup of tea. The form is exact: one stone (not rock), a cup of tea (not coffee). These are for conversation, chats, speeches and columns; a formal report uses plain words (a piece of cake → straightforward). Some fixed expressions fit formal writing too: it remains to be seen, by the same token, to all intents and purposes. For what it's worth is modest and spoken, not for reports.

examples.en: I killed two birds with one stone in Surabaya: I met a client and visited my parents.
examples.id: Sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui di Surabaya: aku bertemu klien sekaligus menjenguk orang tuaku.

examples.en: Remote work is a double-edged sword: more freedom, but the working day never really ends.
examples.id: Kerja jarak jauh itu pedang bermata dua: lebih bebas, tapi hari kerja seperti tidak pernah selesai.

examples.en: Board report: The board found the quarterly results straightforward.
examples.id: Laporan direksi: Dewan direksi menilai hasil kuartalan itu mudah dipahami.

id.title: Peribahasa dan ungkapan baku: bentuk persis, register yang tepat
id.explanation: Peribahasa: the last straw (kesabaran akhirnya habis), a blessing in disguise (buruk di awal, ternyata ada hikmahnya), a double-edged sword (pedang bermata dua: ada untung dan ruginya), a drop in the ocean (terlalu kecil untuk berarti), the elephant in the room (masalah besar yang tidak dibicarakan), move the goalposts (mengubah aturan main di tengah jalan), kill two birds with one stone (sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui), not my cup of tea (bukan seleraku). Bentuknya persis: one stone (bukan rock), a cup of tea (bukan coffee). Ini untuk obrolan, chat, pidato dan kolom opini; laporan formal memakai kata-kata biasa (a piece of cake → straightforward). Beberapa ungkapan baku cocok juga untuk tulisan formal: it remains to be seen, by the same token, to all intents and purposes. For what it's worth bernada rendah hati dan lisan, bukan untuk laporan.

keyPoints.title: How native speakers shorten, adapt and play with idioms
keyPoints.explanation: Native speakers shorten well-known sayings (Speak of the devil…, When in Rome…, the last straw from 'the straw that broke the camel's back'), use standard variants (the last / final straw, a drop in the ocean / in the bucket), adapt them for effect (a blessing in disguise → a curse in disguise), take them literally for a joke in ads and headlines (a game changer, literally: it changes your games) and mix them, by accident (it sounds careless) or as a known joke (It's not rocket surgery). Recognise all of these: find the original idiom and what changed. In your own English, use the safe ones (standard variants and short forms) and keep puns for playful contexts where everyone knows the original.

examples.en: Tom, trying durian on his first trip to Medan: 'Well, when in Rome…'
examples.id: Tom, mencoba durian di perjalanan pertamanya ke Medan: 'Yah, di mana bumi dipijak…'

examples.en: Column: For many young workers, the open-plan office has turned out to be a curse in disguise.
examples.id: Kolom: Bagi banyak pekerja muda, kantor tanpa sekat ternyata justru membawa petaka terselubung.

examples.en: Coffee shop post: Tea? Sorry, not our cup of coffee.
examples.id: Unggahan kedai kopi: Teh? Maaf, bukan 'secangkir kopi' kami. (sengaja dipelesetkan dari 'not my cup of tea')

id.title: Cara penutur asli memendekkan, mengubah dan memainkan idiom
id.explanation: Penutur asli memendekkan peribahasa yang sudah terkenal (Speak of the devil…, When in Rome…, the last straw dari 'the straw that broke the camel's back'), memakai variasi baku (the last / final straw, a drop in the ocean / in the bucket), mengubahnya demi efek (a blessing in disguise → a curse in disguise), mengartikannya secara harfiah sebagai lelucon di iklan dan judul berita (a game changer, literally: it changes your games), dan mencampurnya, entah tidak sengaja (terdengar ceroboh) atau sebagai lelucon yang sudah dikenal (It's not rocket surgery). Kenali semuanya: temukan idiom aslinya dan apa yang diubah. Dalam bahasa Inggrismu sendiri, pakai yang aman (variasi baku dan bentuk pendek) dan simpan plesetan untuk konteks santai di mana semua orang tahu idiom aslinya.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: The new cashless parking system is a ___-edged sword: it's faster, but many older drivers find it hard to use.
guidedPractice.hint: pedang bermata dua: Indonesian and English use exactly the same picture here.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: For what it's ___, I think we should launch the app after Lebaran, not before.
guidedPractice.hint: sekadar pendapat saya: a modest way to give your opinion in a meeting or an email.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: Lecturers expect students to reply to emails within two days. By the same ___, students can expect lecturers to do the same.
guidedPractice.hint: dengan logika yang sama: a fixed expression that works in essays and formal arguments.

guidedPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan wants one plain formal word for a ministry report. Replace 'to all intents and purposes': 'To all intents and purposes, the road project is finished.' → ___, the road project is finished.
guidedPractice.hint: pada dasarnya, praktis: one adverb ending in -ly.

guidedPractice.prompt: Dimas writes in the team chat: 'It's not rocket surgery: just send the invoice on time.' This joke mixes two idioms that both mean 'it's not difficult'. Write them, joined by 'and'.
expected: it's not rocket science and it's not brain surgery
it is not rocket science and it is not brain surgery
guidedPractice.hint: One is about space travel, the other about operating on the head.

independentPractice.prompt: Sari about her new company car: 'It looked like a great perk, but the parking fees in Jakarta are huge. A curse in disguise, really.' Which idiom is she playing with? Write it.
independentPractice.hint: She swapped one word for its opposite: something bad that turns out good.

independentPractice.prompt: A gym in Bandung puts up a banner next to its new treadmills: 'We're going the extra mile. Literally.' Is this a mistake or a deliberate joke? Write mistake or joke.
independentPractice.hint: Think about what people actually do on a treadmill, and the C1 idiom go the extra mile.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: Bu Ani's team loves karaoke nights after work, but Sari prefers a quiet evening with a book. Karaoke just isn't her cup of ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: tea (not my cup of tea = bukan seleraku). 'coffee' / 'kopi' = 0: the idiom is fixed, and coffee is the typical Indonesian slip. 'thing' / 'style' = 20 (the right idea, but not the idiom). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: First the client asked for a 10% discount. When we agreed, they asked for 20% and free delivery to Makassar. They keep moving the ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: goalposts (also written goal posts; move the goalposts = mengubah aturan main di tengah jalan). 'goalpost' = 60 (right idiom, but it's plural: there are two posts). 'goals' / 'target' / 'targets' = 30 (the right idea, but not the idiom). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: At the budget meeting, everyone talked about printer paper and the coffee machine. Nobody mentioned the 30% cut to the training budget, although everyone knew about it. The cut was the ___ in the room.
assessment.rubric: Correct: elephant (the elephant in the room = masalah besar yang semua orang tahu tapi tidak dibicarakan). 'elephants' = 60 (the idiom is singular). 'problem' / 'issue' = 20 (the right idea, but not the idiom). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rina is writing the annual report for the board of directors. Her draft says: 'The six-month delay to the factory permit proved a blessing in disguise: it gave the engineers time to redesign the cooling system.' Replace 'a blessing in disguise' with plain, formal words (one to three words).
assessment.rubric: Correct: any plain, formal word or phrase meaning 'turned out to have a good result' that fits after 'proved' (beneficial, advantageous, fortunate, an unexpected benefit, useful …). 'good' / 'lucky' / 'a good thing' = 50 (right meaning, but too informal or vague for a board report). Another idiom (a godsend, a silver lining) = 20 (still an idiom). Anything that means bad = 0.

assessment.prompt: A travel agency in Denpasar posts this ad for foreign tourists: 'When in Bali, do as the Balinese do: join a cooking class and make your own sate lilit!' Which well-known English saying is the ad playing with? Write the original saying.
acceptableAnswers: when in rome do as the romans do
when in rome do as romans do
when you are in rome do as the romans do
when you're in rome do as the romans do
assessment.rubric: Correct: When in Rome, do as the Romans do (the short form 'When in Rome' is also full marks; ≈ di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung). A correct explanation of the meaning without the saying (follow local customs) = 40. 'di mana bumi dipijak di situ langit dijunjung' alone = 30 (the right Indonesian twin, but the task asks for the English saying). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: The full saying is 'It's the straw that broke the camel's back', but native speakers usually shorten it. Complete with one word: The client changed the deadline for the fourth time in a week, and that was the ___ straw: Pak Hasan ended the contract.
assessment.rubric: Correct: last or final (the last straw and the final straw are both standard). 'only' / 'end' / 'lastest' = 0. Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: An electric scooter rental app in Jakarta has this slogan: 'New job tomorrow? Hit the ground rolling.' Which idiom is the slogan playing with? Write the original idiom.
assessment.rubric: Correct: hit the ground running (langsung tancap gas from the first day; the scooter's wheels roll instead of the runner's feet). A correct explanation of the meaning without the idiom (start well from the first day) = 40. Another idiom = 0.

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** you know that an **idiom** is a fixed group of words you learn as one piece, that its words are fixed but the grammar around it changes (*It **paid** off*), and that plain words work better in formal reports. At C2 you add **sayings** (peribahasa: short, well-known sentences or phrases about life) whose form must be **exact**, and you learn to judge where each one fits.

- **the last straw** = the last of many small problems, the one that finally makes you lose patience (kesabaran habis). It's short for *the straw that broke the camel's back*: one more straw (jerami) and the camel's back breaks.
- **a blessing in disguise** = something that looks bad at first but turns out good (ada hikmahnya). *Disguise* = penyamaran.
- **a double-edged sword** = something with clear advantages AND clear disadvantages.
- **a drop in the ocean** = an amount far too small to make a difference (tidak seberapa). American English also says *a drop in the bucket*.
- **the elephant in the room** = a big, obvious problem that everyone knows about but nobody mentions.
- **move the goalposts** = change the rules or the target in the middle of a process, usually unfairly (mengubah aturan main di tengah jalan). Always a complaint about someone else.
- **kill two birds with one stone** = get two things done with one action.
- **not my cup of tea** = not something I like (bukan seleraku). Almost always negative.

**Register** (tingkat formalitas): all eight are fine in conversation, chats, speeches and opinion columns. *a double-edged sword*, *a drop in the ocean* and *the elephant in the room* also appear in serious journalism. In a formal report, plain words are still safer.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat:** kamu sudah tahu bahwa **idiom** adalah kelompok kata tetap yang dipelajari sebagai satu kesatuan, bahwa kata-katanya tetap tapi tata bahasa di sekitarnya berubah (*It **paid** off*), dan bahwa kata-kata biasa lebih baik di laporan formal. Di level C2 kamu menambah **peribahasa** (kalimat atau frasa pendek yang terkenal tentang kehidupan) yang bentuknya harus **persis**, dan belajar menilai di mana masing-masing cocok.

- **the last straw** = masalah kecil terakhir dari sekian banyak masalah, yang akhirnya membuat kesabaranmu habis. Ini kependekan dari *the straw that broke the camel's back*: satu helai jerami lagi, dan punggung untanya patah.
- **a blessing in disguise** = sesuatu yang awalnya terlihat buruk tapi ternyata baik (ada hikmahnya). *Disguise* = penyamaran.
- **a double-edged sword** = sesuatu yang punya kelebihan DAN kekurangan yang sama-sama jelas.
- **a drop in the ocean** = jumlah yang terlalu kecil untuk membawa perubahan (tidak seberapa). Bahasa Inggris Amerika juga memakai *a drop in the bucket*.
- **the elephant in the room** = masalah besar dan jelas yang semua orang tahu tapi tidak ada yang membicarakannya.
- **move the goalposts** = mengubah aturan main atau target di tengah jalan, biasanya dengan tidak adil. Selalu dipakai untuk mengeluhkan pihak lain.
- **kill two birds with one stone** = menyelesaikan dua hal dengan satu tindakan.
- **not my cup of tea** = bukan sesuatu yang aku suka (bukan seleraku). Hampir selalu dalam kalimat negatif.

**Register** (tingkat formalitas): kedelapannya cocok untuk obrolan, chat, pidato dan kolom opini. *a double-edged sword*, *a drop in the ocean* dan *the elephant in the room* juga muncul di jurnalisme yang serius. Di laporan formal, kata-kata biasa tetap lebih aman.

rows.en: When the landlord raised the rent for the third time this year, that was the last straw: we moved out.
rows.id: Waktu pemilik kos menaikkan sewa untuk ketiga kalinya tahun ini, kesabaran kami habis: kami pindah.

rows.en: Missing that flight was a blessing in disguise: I met my future business partner at the airport.
rows.id: Ketinggalan pesawat itu ternyata ada hikmahnya: aku bertemu calon mitra bisnisku di bandara.

rows.en: Rp 10 million is a drop in the ocean for a bank that size.
rows.id: Rp 10 juta itu tidak seberapa untuk bank sebesar itu.

rows.en: Nobody wanted to mention the elephant in the room: the project was already six months late.
rows.id: Tidak ada yang mau menyebut masalah besar yang sudah jelas itu: proyeknya sudah terlambat enam bulan.

rows.en: Halfway through the tender, the ministry moved the goalposts and added three new requirements.
rows.id: Di tengah proses tender, kementerian mengubah aturan main dan menambah tiga syarat baru.

rows.en: Horror films aren't really my cup of tea.
rows.id: Film horor sebenarnya bukan seleraku.

blocks.text:
**Indonesian bridges and traps.**
- *a double-edged sword* = **pedang bermata dua**: a true twin, same picture, same meaning.
- *kill two birds with one stone* ≈ **sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui**: the same idea, a different picture (a stone instead of rowing). **Trap:** *batu* can be *stone* or *rock*, but the idiom is fixed: **one stone**, never 'one rock'.
- *not my cup of tea*: Indonesia is a coffee country, so 'not my cup of coffee' feels natural. It isn't: the idiom is always **tea**. Change it and a listener thinks you've made a mistake (unless the context makes it an obvious joke: more on that later).

id.text:
**Jembatan dan jebakan dari bahasa Indonesia.**
- *a double-edged sword* = **pedang bermata dua**: kembaran sejati, gambarannya sama, artinya sama.
- *kill two birds with one stone* ≈ **sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui**: idenya sama, gambarannya beda (batu, bukan mendayung). **Jebakan:** *batu* bisa *stone* atau *rock*, tapi idiomnya tetap: **one stone**, tidak pernah 'one rock'.
- *not my cup of tea*: Indonesia negeri kopi, jadi 'not my cup of coffee' terasa wajar. Padahal tidak: idiomnya selalu **tea**. Kalau kamu menggantinya, pendengar akan mengira kamu salah (kecuali konteksnya jelas-jelas bercanda: nanti dibahas).

blocks.prompt: In a meeting about a new e-ticket system, Pak Hasan says: 'For our passengers, this system is a double-edged sword.' What does he mean?
options: It has clear advantages and clear disadvantages for passengers.
It is dangerous for passengers and should be stopped.
It is very strong and will work faster than the old one.
blocks.explain: a double-edged sword = pedang bermata dua: it helps in one way and hurts in another. It's not about danger or strength: read the idiom as one piece.

id.prompt: Dalam rapat tentang sistem tiket elektronik yang baru, Pak Hasan berkata: 'For our passengers, this system is a double-edged sword.' Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: a double-edged sword = pedang bermata dua: membantu di satu sisi, merugikan di sisi lain. Ini bukan soal bahaya atau kekuatan: baca idiomnya sebagai satu kesatuan.

material.title: Fixed expressions for formal writing, and when to drop the idiom

id.title: Ungkapan baku untuk tulisan formal, dan kapan idiom harus ditinggalkan

blocks.text:
Not every fixed expression is informal. These four are fixed too, but they have no colourful picture, so most of them work in reports, essays and serious journalism:
- **it remains to be seen (whether …)** = we can't know yet (masih harus dilihat, belum pasti). Perfect for cautious reports.
- **by the same token** = for the same reason, following the same logic (dengan logika yang sama, begitu pula). Common in arguments and essays.
- **to all intents and purposes** = in practice, almost completely (pada dasarnya, praktis). American English often says *for all intents and purposes*. Careful: people sometimes write 'to all intensive purposes' because it sounds similar. It's wrong.
- **for what it's worth** = I'm not sure how useful this is, but here's my opinion (sekadar pendapat saya). Modest and friendly: good in meetings and emails, **not** in a formal report.

The other side of register: a **colourful idiom** (one with a picture: cake, straws, elephants, goalposts) in a formal report sounds like a chat message. Replace it with a plain word:
- *a piece of cake* → **straightforward**, *easy*
- *a drop in the ocean* → **negligible**, *insignificant*
- *the last straw* → **the final factor that led to …**

id.text:
Tidak semua ungkapan baku itu santai. Empat ungkapan ini juga tetap bentuknya, tapi tidak punya gambaran yang 'warna-warni', jadi sebagian besar cocok untuk laporan, esai dan jurnalisme yang serius:
- **it remains to be seen (whether …)** = kita belum bisa tahu (masih harus dilihat, belum pasti). Sangat cocok untuk laporan yang berhati-hati.
- **by the same token** = dengan alasan yang sama, mengikuti logika yang sama (begitu pula). Sering muncul dalam argumen dan esai.
- **to all intents and purposes** = pada praktiknya, hampir sepenuhnya (pada dasarnya, praktis). Bahasa Inggris Amerika sering memakai *for all intents and purposes*. Hati-hati: orang kadang menulis 'to all intensive purposes' karena bunyinya mirip. Itu salah.
- **for what it's worth** = aku tidak yakin ini berguna, tapi ini pendapatku (sekadar pendapat saya). Rendah hati dan ramah: cocok di rapat dan email, **bukan** di laporan formal.

Sisi lain dari register: **idiom bergambar** (yang punya gambaran: kue, jerami, gajah, tiang gawang) di laporan formal terdengar seperti pesan chat. Gantilah dengan kata biasa:
- *a piece of cake* → **straightforward**, *easy*
- *a drop in the ocean* → **negligible**, *insignificant*
- *the last straw* → **the final factor that led to …**

rows.en: Report: Whether the new subsidy will reach rural families remains to be seen.
rows.id: Laporan: Apakah subsidi baru ini akan sampai ke keluarga di desa masih harus dilihat.

rows.en: Essay: Cities must invest in buses. By the same token, they must stop building new car parks.
rows.id: Esai: Kota harus berinvestasi pada bus. Dengan logika yang sama, kota harus berhenti membangun lahan parkir baru.

rows.en: News: The merger means that, to all intents and purposes, the two airlines are now one company.
rows.id: Berita: Merger itu berarti, pada dasarnya, kedua maskapai sekarang adalah satu perusahaan.

rows.en: Email to a colleague: For what it's worth, I thought your presentation was excellent.
rows.id: Email ke rekan kerja: Sekadar pendapatku, presentasimu tadi sangat bagus.

rows.en: Board report: The board found the quarterly results straightforward.
rows.id: Laporan direksi: Dewan direksi menilai hasil kuartalan itu mudah dipahami.

blocks.text: **The classic C2 slip:** *The board thought the quarterly results were a piece of cake.* The grammar is perfect, the idiom is correct, and it's still wrong, because a board report is formal. Write **The board found the quarterly results straightforward.** The question at C2 is not only *Is it correct?* but *Does it fit this reader?* When you aren't sure, choose the plain word: it's never wrong in formal writing.

id.text: **Kekeliruan klasik di level C2:** *The board thought the quarterly results were a piece of cake.* Tata bahasanya sempurna, idiomnya benar, tapi tetap salah, karena laporan direksi itu formal. Tulis **The board found the quarterly results straightforward.** Pertanyaan di level C2 bukan hanya *Apakah ini benar?* tapi juga *Apakah ini cocok untuk pembaca ini?* Kalau ragu, pilih kata biasa: itu tidak pernah salah dalam tulisan formal.

blocks.prompt: Dr. Wulan is writing a formal policy brief about import tariffs. Which expression fits? 'The new 200% tariff is, ___, a ban on imported steel.'
blocks.explain: to all intents and purposes = in practice (pada dasarnya): a 200% tariff works like a ban. 'intensive purposes' is a well-known mishearing, not the expression. 'for what it's worth' introduces a modest personal opinion: fine in an email, but wrong in meaning and register here.

id.prompt: Dr. Wulan sedang menulis ringkasan kebijakan formal tentang tarif impor. Ungkapan mana yang cocok? 'The new 200% tariff is, ___, a ban on imported steel.'
id.explain: to all intents and purposes = pada praktiknya (pada dasarnya): tarif 200% berfungsi seperti larangan. 'intensive purposes' adalah salah dengar yang terkenal, bukan ungkapannya. 'for what it's worth' membuka pendapat pribadi yang rendah hati: cocok di email, tapi salah makna dan salah register di sini.

id.title: Peribahasa yang dipendekkan dan variasi baku

blocks.text:
"The words are fixed" is the rule for learners, but native speakers do bend some idioms, in a few predictable ways. Knowing them helps you **recognise** what you hear and read.

**1. Shortening.** When a saying is very well known, people say only the first half and let the listener finish it in their head:
- **Speak of the devil** (… and he shall appear) = said when the person you were just talking about walks in. Light-hearted, not rude. Indonesian says **Panjang umur!** in the same moment, but don't translate it: 'Long life!' means nothing in English.
- **When in Rome** (… do as the Romans do) = follow the local customs ≈ **di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung**.
- **the last straw** is itself a short form of *the straw that broke the camel's back*.

**2. Standard variants.** Some idioms have two accepted forms: **the last straw / the final straw**, **a drop in the ocean / a drop in the bucket** (American), **to all intents and purposes / for all intents and purposes**. And normal grammar still works: *The goalposts **keep moving**.* *That **was** the final straw.*

**3. Adapting for effect.** Writers swap one word to create a new meaning the reader can still decode: *a blessing in disguise* → **a curse in disguise** (it looked good, but turned out bad). This works only because everyone knows the original.

id.text:
"Kata-katanya tetap" adalah aturan untuk pelajar, tapi penutur asli memang membengkokkan sebagian idiom, dengan beberapa cara yang bisa ditebak. Mengetahuinya membantumu **mengenali** apa yang kamu dengar dan baca.

**1. Dipendekkan.** Kalau sebuah peribahasa sangat terkenal, orang hanya mengucapkan separuh pertamanya dan membiarkan pendengar melanjutkannya di kepala:
- **Speak of the devil** (… and he shall appear) = diucapkan saat orang yang baru saja dibicarakan muncul. Bernada bercanda, tidak kasar. Dalam bahasa Indonesia kita bilang **Panjang umur!** di momen yang sama, tapi jangan diterjemahkan: 'Long life!' tidak bermakna apa-apa dalam bahasa Inggris.
- **When in Rome** (… do as the Romans do) = ikuti kebiasaan setempat ≈ **di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung**.
- **the last straw** sendiri adalah bentuk pendek dari *the straw that broke the camel's back*.

**2. Variasi baku.** Beberapa idiom punya dua bentuk yang sama-sama diterima: **the last straw / the final straw**, **a drop in the ocean / a drop in the bucket** (Amerika), **to all intents and purposes / for all intents and purposes**. Dan tata bahasa biasa tetap berlaku: *The goalposts **keep moving**.* *That **was** the final straw.*

**3. Diubah demi efek.** Penulis menukar satu kata untuk menciptakan makna baru yang masih bisa ditebak pembaca: *a blessing in disguise* → **a curse in disguise** (kelihatannya baik, ternyata buruk). Ini hanya berhasil karena semua orang tahu bentuk aslinya.

rows.en: Tom, trying durian on his first trip to Medan: 'Well, when in Rome…'
rows.id: Tom, mencoba durian di perjalanan pertamanya ke Medan: 'Yah, di mana bumi dipijak…'

rows.en: The supplier missed the delivery date again, and that was the final straw.
rows.id: Pemasok itu lagi-lagi melewatkan tanggal pengiriman, dan kesabaran kami pun habis.

rows.en: With this client, the goalposts keep moving.
rows.id: Dengan klien ini, aturan mainnya terus berubah.

rows.en: Column: For many young workers, the open-plan office has turned out to be a curse in disguise.
rows.id: Kolom: Bagi banyak pekerja muda, kantor tanpa sekat ternyata justru membawa petaka terselubung.

blocks.text: **Indonesian does this too.** You often hear just *Sekali mendayung…* or *Di mana bumi dipijak…*, and everyone finishes the saying in their head. English works the same way: the half you hear is a signal for the whole saying. But you can only shorten sayings that are famous; don't cut a C1 idiom in half (*'Let's clear the…'* doesn't work).

id.text: **Bahasa Indonesia juga begitu.** Kamu sering mendengar orang hanya bilang *Sekali mendayung…* atau *Di mana bumi dipijak…*, dan semua orang melanjutkan peribahasanya di kepala. Bahasa Inggris juga sama: separuh yang kamu dengar adalah tanda untuk keseluruhan peribahasanya. Tapi yang bisa dipendekkan hanya peribahasa yang sangat terkenal; jangan memotong idiom C1 di tengah (*'Let's clear the…'* tidak bisa).

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani says in a meeting: 'They've changed the specifications again. Well, that's the final straw.' Is 'final' correct here?
options: No: the idiom is fixed, so only 'the last straw' is correct.
Yes: 'the final straw' is a standard variant of 'the last straw'.
No: it should be 'the final straws'.
blocks.explain: Most idioms are fixed, but a few have two standard forms, and the last straw / the final straw is one of them. The noun stays singular: one straw breaks the camel's back.

id.prompt: Bu Ani berkata dalam rapat: 'They've changed the specifications again. Well, that's the final straw.' Apakah 'final' benar di sini?
id.explain: Sebagian besar idiom itu tetap, tapi ada beberapa yang punya dua bentuk baku, dan the last straw / the final straw salah satunya. Kata bendanya tetap tunggal: satu helai jerami yang mematahkan punggung unta.

material.title: Literal jokes, puns and mixed metaphors

id.title: Lelucon harfiah, plesetan dan metafora campur

blocks.text:
**4. Taking an idiom literally.** Ads and headlines love to use an idiom's real, physical meaning (makna harfiah) for a joke. The word **literally** often signals it:
- Phone ad: *This new phone really is a **game changer**: literally, it changes your games.* (*a game changer* = something that changes a situation completely; here the phone actually changes video games.)
- Headline: *Stadium works begin: the club **moves the goalposts**, literally.* (the builders really move the goals.)

**5. Puns** (plesetan): one word is swapped for a similar-sounding word that fits the context. A coffee shop writes *Tea? Sorry, not our cup of **coffee**.* That's deliberate: it's a coffee shop, and the swap is the joke.

**6. Mixed metaphors** (metafora campur: two idioms with different pictures in one sentence).
- **By accident**, it sounds careless: *The merger is a double-edged sword that will kill two birds with one stone.* (A sword and a stone in one picture: the reader stops and frowns.)
- **On purpose**, as a known joke: *It's not rocket surgery* mixes *it's not rocket science* and *it's not brain surgery*. Both mean 'it isn't difficult', and the mix makes the speaker sound playful.

**How to read a twist:** ask three questions. What is the original idiom? What changed? Why does the change make sense in this context?

id.text:
**4. Mengartikan idiom secara harfiah.** Iklan dan judul berita suka memakai makna harfiah (makna fisik yang sebenarnya) dari sebuah idiom untuk bercanda. Kata **literally** sering menjadi tandanya:
- Iklan ponsel: *This new phone really is a **game changer**: literally, it changes your games.* (*a game changer* = sesuatu yang mengubah keadaan sepenuhnya; di sini ponselnya benar-benar mengubah game.)
- Judul berita: *Stadium works begin: the club **moves the goalposts**, literally.* (para pekerja benar-benar memindahkan tiang gawangnya.)

**5. Plesetan**: satu kata ditukar dengan kata yang bunyinya mirip dan cocok dengan konteks. Sebuah kedai kopi menulis *Tea? Sorry, not our cup of **coffee**.* Itu disengaja: tempatnya kedai kopi, dan pertukarannya adalah leluconnya.

**6. Metafora campur** (dua idiom dengan gambaran berbeda dalam satu kalimat).
- **Tidak sengaja**, terdengar ceroboh: *The merger is a double-edged sword that will kill two birds with one stone.* (Pedang dan batu dalam satu gambaran: pembaca berhenti dan mengernyit.)
- **Sengaja**, sebagai lelucon yang sudah dikenal: *It's not rocket surgery* mencampur *it's not rocket science* dan *it's not brain surgery*. Keduanya berarti 'ini tidak sulit', dan campurannya membuat pembicara terdengar jenaka.

**Cara membaca sebuah plesetan:** ajukan tiga pertanyaan. Apa idiom aslinya? Apa yang diubah? Kenapa perubahan itu masuk akal dalam konteks ini?

rows.en: Report draft: The merger is a double-edged sword that will kill two birds with one stone.
rows.id: Draf laporan: Merger ini pedang bermata dua yang akan menyelesaikan dua masalah sekaligus.

blocks.text: **Recognise everything, produce the safe ones.** A twist works only when (1) the audience knows the original and (2) the context gives the change a reason. The coffee shop's 'not our cup of coffee' is clever; the same words from you in a job interview ('Accounting isn't really my cup of coffee') just sound like a mistake. In your own English, use standard variants and short forms freely. Keep puns and literal jokes for ads, toasts and team chats, and never put them in a formal report or use them with people whose English is limited.

id.text: **Kenali semuanya, pakai yang aman.** Sebuah plesetan hanya berhasil kalau (1) pendengar tahu bentuk aslinya dan (2) konteksnya memberi alasan untuk perubahan itu. 'not our cup of coffee' dari kedai kopi itu cerdas; kata-kata yang sama darimu saat wawancara kerja ('Accounting isn't really my cup of coffee') hanya terdengar seperti kesalahan. Dalam bahasa Inggrismu sendiri, pakai variasi baku dan bentuk pendek dengan bebas. Simpan plesetan dan lelucon harfiah untuk iklan, sambutan dan chat tim, dan jangan pernah memakainya di laporan formal atau dengan orang yang bahasa Inggrisnya terbatas.

blocks.prompt: In a job interview at a bank, Dimas says: 'Accounting isn't really my cup of coffee, so I'd prefer the marketing role.' What's going on?
options: A clever joke: it shows great control of English.
Correct American English: Americans say coffee.
A mistake: the idiom is 'my cup of tea', and nothing in the context makes 'coffee' a joke.
blocks.explain: not my cup of tea is fixed in British and American English. A swap is a joke only when the context explains it (a coffee shop's post); in an interview it just sounds like a slip.

id.prompt: Dalam wawancara kerja di sebuah bank, Dimas berkata: 'Accounting isn't really my cup of coffee, so I'd prefer the marketing role.' Apa yang terjadi?
id.explain: not my cup of tea itu tetap, baik dalam bahasa Inggris Inggris maupun Amerika. Pertukaran kata baru menjadi lelucon kalau konteksnya menjelaskannya (unggahan kedai kopi); di wawancara, itu hanya terdengar seperti salah ucap.

resources.title: Smoke and mirrors (Newspaper idioms)
resources.note: Kate Woodford explains nine idioms found in British newspapers on a single day (smoke and mirrors, raise the bar, a perfect storm, cut off your nose to spite your face …), each with a real example. None of them are in this lesson, so it's extra practice in reading idioms the way journalists use them. British English, all in English.

id.note: Kate Woodford menjelaskan sembilan idiom yang ditemukan di surat kabar Inggris pada satu hari yang sama (smoke and mirrors, raise the bar, a perfect storm, cut off your nose to spite your face …), masing-masing dengan contoh nyata. Tidak ada yang dari pelajaran ini, jadi ini latihan tambahan membaca idiom seperti yang dipakai jurnalis. Bahasa Inggris Inggris, seluruhnya dalam bahasa Inggris.

id.intro: Kamu sudah memakai idiom seperti cut corners dan pay off, dan tahu kapan kata-kata biasa lebih baik. Sekarang lapisan C2: peribahasa dengan bentuk yang persis (kill two birds with one stone, tidak pernah 'one rock'), ungkapan baku yang bahkan cocok untuk laporan formal, dan cara penutur asli memendekkan, memelesetkan dan bercanda dengan idiom. Pemanasan: ingat satu kejadian buruk yang akhirnya justru baik untukmu.
